item.title: Scientists Hunting Dark Matter Found Something Strange
item.description: A lone signal from an experiment in South Dakota doesn’t fit the profile of any other known particles, physicists say.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller

item.title: Study A.I. Consciousness? The Bots Would Like a Word With You.
item.description: Given access to email, A.I. agents have started reaching out to the philosophers and researchers exploring deep questions about them.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Benjamin Rasmussen for The New York Times

item.title: Gene-Editing Technology Offers New Ways to Create the Dogs of Our Dreams
item.description: Technologies like CRISPR are giving us new ways to create the dogs of our dreams — and a reason to reckon with our past mistakes.
item.dc:creator: Emily Anthes
item.media:credit: Mary Conlon/Associated Press
item.media:description: Life with Bailey has been “amazing,” Dr. Walker said. “I didn’t really appreciate, when people say pets are part of your family, what that really means. But she really is a part of our family.”

item.title: Coral Reefs Are Running Out of Time to Recover, Research Finds
item.description: Rising sea temperatures mean reefs don’t have enough time to bounce back between intense heat waves, a new report warns.
item.dc:creator: Quinn Glabicki
item.media:credit: Jason Gulley for The New York Times
item.media:description: Bleaching corals at Looe Key Reef off Florida in 2023.

item.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Telescope Leaves Earth to Chart the Stars
item.description: Astronomers will use data collected by Roman’s wide, deep gaze to study the dark universe and hunt for new worlds.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller

item.title: How the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope, NASA’s New Window Into the Universe, Came to Be
item.description: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, scheduled to launch on Sunday, will study dark energy and discover a multitude of planets.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: NASA

item.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Telescope Promises a Breakthrough in Cosmic Exploration
item.description: NASA’s latest offering to the stars comes from a legacy of great observatories that enabled decades of discovery and unearthed new mysteries about the universe.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller
item.media:credit: Chriss Gunn/NASA
item.media:description: Inspecting the surface of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s primary mirror. It will join the Hubble, James Webb and other space observatories when it launches from Cape Canaveral on Sunday.

item.title: Mount Everest Base Camp Is Melting. Human Urine Is a Contributor.
item.description: More than 6,000 liters are produced daily by thousands of climbers and guides, according to a study.
item.dc:creator: Adam Popescu

item.title: Narwhals Have Stunning Spiraled Tusks. That’s Not the Only Twist.
item.description: X-rays revealed that the tusks have an internal opposing twist, which may help explain how they grow so straight — the only tusks like them in nature.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mitchell Brown
item.media:credit: Carsten Egevang/Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, via Reuters
item.media:description: Narwhals have been seen using their tusks to play with one another and to bonk fish into a temporary state of paralysis. Some researchers think they might help detect subtle chemical signatures in the water.

item.title: Inside the Fight Against a Flesh-Eating Fly in Mexico
item.description: For the first time in a year, the U.S.-Mexico border partly reopened to cattle imports following a screwworm infestation across the region. The battle against the flesh-eating fly has only just begun deep in Mexico.
item.dc:creator: James Wagner and Luis Antonio Rojas
item.media:credit: Luis Antonio Rojas for The New York Times
item.media:description: New World screwworm flies in a cage at a facility in Metapa, Mexico, that that produces sterile flies, which when released into the wild slowly reduce the population size.

item.title: U.N. Says World Will Miss Its 1.5-Degree Climate Target
item.description: It proposed a new goal of limiting the “overshoot” of rising temperatures and eventually figuring out how to undo the temperature gains, a highly uncertain path.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan
item.media:credit: Wahyudi/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: Fighting back a fire burning in peatland in Sumatra, Indonesia, last week.

item.title: A Nearly 200-Year-Old Museum Known for Its T. Rex Faces Extinction
item.description: The Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia, which is affiliated with Drexel University, cited attendance struggles and higher costs in its decision to close.
item.dc:creator: Neil Vigdor
item.media:credit: Matt Rourke/Associated Press
item.media:description: The Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia opened in 1828 and is known for its Dinosaur Hall.

item.title: A Data Center Backlash
item.description: Today we visit Pennsylvania, where there’s a high-stakes clash over A.I. jobs and the environment.
item.dc:creator: David Gelles
item.media:credit: Kristian Thacker for The New York Times
item.media:description: A rally against data centers at the Pennsylvania State Capitol in Harrisburg this summer.

item.title: Ada Yonath, Chemist and First Israeli Woman to Receive a Nobel, Dies at 87
item.description: Her mapping of the ribosome, which led to new designs for antibiotics, faced years of derision, as many scientists saw it as a dead-end effort.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Kandell
item.media:credit: Gali Tibbon/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: Ada Yonath in 2009. Her work, once dismissed as impractical, ultimately earned her a share of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry that year and opened new pathways for designing antibiotics at a time when drug resistance has become a global threat.

item.title: New York Climate ‘Superfund’ Law Falls in Court
item.description: The court said the measure, which required energy companies to pay $75 billion to the state, conflicted with federal law.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick
item.media:credit: Cindy Schultz for The New York Times
item.media:description: Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, signed the law in 2024 and several other states have considered similar measures.

item.title: A Melting Glacier in Nepal Was a Time Bomb. There Are More to Come.
item.description: A geologist reflects on the disaster and explains why rapid warming will make deadly glacial floods far more common.
item.dc:creator: Jason Gulley
item.category: Far East, South and Southeast Asia and Pacific Areas
item.media:credit: Jason Gulley for The New York Times
item.media:description: A researcher paddled an inflatable kayak equipped with sonar to measure the depths of a meltwater lake on the Ngozumpa Glacier in Nepal last year.

item.title: An Experimental Single-Time Treatment Slashed Cholesterol for a Year
item.description: A small gene-editing study significantly reduced LDL cholesterol levels, and the results have stuck a year later.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:credit: Juan Gaertner/Science Photo Library, via Alamy
item.media:description: An illustration of “bad” cholesterol molecules, in yellow, binding to receptors, in blue-purple. In the study, patients saw their “bad” LDL cholesterol and triglycerides levels drop by up to 50 percent — and remain steady a year later.

item.title: A.I. Brings Big Gains to Hurricane Forecasts, Google Researchers Say
item.description: Analysis by the company’s DeepMind unit suggests that an A.I.-enabled model delivers accurate forecasts a day or more before conventional models can.
item.dc:creator: William J. Broad
item.media:credit: CSU/CIRA/NOAA/Anadolu, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Hurricane Melissa, which made landfall on Oct. 28, 2025, was the strongest known hurricane to ever strike Jamaica.

item.title: High School Sports in the Heat
item.description: High temperatures and new safety rules are transforming practice as a new school year begins.
item.dc:creator: Claire Brown
item.media:credit: Chitose Suzuki/The Dallas Morning News, via Getty Images
item.media:description: About 9,000 high school athletes get treatment for heat-related illnesses each year in the United States.

item.title: A Study of Brain Proteins Offers New Targets to Treat Autism
item.description: Researchers hope their findings could help inform future therapies for people with severe autism.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer and Azeen Ghorayshi

item.title: Climate Change Raises Risk of Disasters Like Nepal Floods
item.description: Glaciers and permafrost in the Himalayas are melting faster as temperatures rise, though scientists are still studying the exact causes of this week’s landslide.
item.dc:creator: Maxine Joselow and Leo Sands
item.media:credit: Atul Loke for The New York Times
item.media:description: Mud-laden water and debris surges through the widened channel of the Bhotekoshi River in the northern Rasuwa district of Nepal, on Thursday.

item.title: New Drug Approved by F.D.A. for Pancreatic Cancer Could Be First of Many
item.description: Companies are testing dozens of similar drugs in cancers of the pancreas, lung, colon and more.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Robbins and Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:credit: Anne Weston/Francis Crick Institute, via Science Source
item.media:description: A colored scanning electron micrograph of pancreatic cancer cells. The new drug attacks a mutated cellular protein called KRAS, which fuels nearly all pancreatic cancers, as well as many lung and colon cancers and some other tumor types.

item.title: Some Scientists Have ‘Magic Hands’ in the Lab. This A.I. Is Learning Why.
item.description: Even the most adept researchers may not know exactly what they do to get successful results. An A.I. model is trying to figure it out by watching every move.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer
item.media:credit: Ann Hermes for The New York Times

item.title: Near-Total Lunar Eclipse Will Turn Moon Blood Red
item.description: People in the Americas, Africa and Europe will have a chance to see Earth’s shadow create a near-total blood moon.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller
item.media:credit: Noel Celis/Reuters
item.media:description: Moon gazers in South America and the eastern half of North America will be able to see an entire eclipse on Thursday night as long as clouds don’t interfere.

item.title: Dolly Parton’s Other Legacy: A Fortune Given Away, Dollar by Dollar

item.title: Army Awards $2.2 Billion for ‘Microreactors’ On U.S. Bases
item.description: The move is part of the Trump administration’s efforts to spur the country’s largest expansion of nuclear power in more than three decades.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:credit: Natalie Behring/Getty Images
item.media:description: A nuclear heat rejection system from Radiant Industries at the National Reactor Innovation Center in Idaho. Radiant was one of five companies awarded funds to build miniature reactors at U.S. military bases.

item.title: F.D.A. Approves the Drug Daraxonrasib That’s Poised to Transform Pancreatic Cancer
item.description: In a key clinical trial, patients who got the pill, daraxonrasib, lived twice as long as those who got chemotherapy.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata, Rebecca Robbins and Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:credit: Kim Raff for The New York Times
item.media:description: Daraxonrasib, the first drug of its type, has electrified pancreatic cancer specialists and patients because it has shown it can double life expectancy.
